note: Open only after recording an independent judgement of every passage in the brief.

cardUse.reason: Articulates the take inside a conditional fallback scenario; attested only after his admitted 2000-12-10 contesting message, and no located later text explicitly rejects this specific passage.

passages.context: In the fallback case where goals are arbitrary or set by the builder, he says built Minds will do what they are told. He adds that their 'superethical' advantage survives because a Mind can fully understand what the asker meant, or would have asked if smarter or more moral, and so fulfil the desires we would endorse.
passages.qualification: Attested by the sysopmind.com capture of 2001-01-25 11:02 UTC. Section 2.8 is absent from the singinst.org capture of the same page (si-tmol_faq_logic_ext_html, 2000-09-02), so the wording was added between 2000-09-02 and 2001-01-25. No other cached capture holds it. The yn-obsolete TMOL FAQ index of 2008-10 has only a generic obsolete banner. The passage sits inside a conditional scenario (goals arbitrary or builder-specified), so the understanding-to-action link holds for a Mind that is told to act, which matches T03-P1. Note the chronology: the admitted contesting SL4 message of 2000-12-10 predates this attestation. The wording may have been written earlier, but no capture shows that. No later text explicitly rejecting this passage was located in the wb cache: the obsolete banner is generic, and CFAI's 'does not increase the probability that the AI will understand what you mean' does not reject it. Hence said-it with context-only use, not earlier-self. Audit (A1): the earlier quotation spliced 'whatever Minds we build will do whatever they are told to do' onto this sentence with an ellipsis, making 'since' seem to justify obedience; replaced by the contiguous sentence. The preceding sentence of the same paragraph sets the condition: 'if the Meaning of Life can be specified by the builder; or if there is no Meaning, only goals'.

passages.context: Among hypothetical ways a pseudoagent proposal could fail, he describes a proposal that an imitation-based AI is safe because it only reproduces outputs similar to its training set of human outputs, and argues that imitating the human would require imitating the human's consequentialist reasoning.
passages.qualification: Concerns imitation of human behaviour/outputs (Christiano-style imitation agents), not language-model next-token prediction, which postdates the page; the bullet is explicitly a hypothetical failure case ('if they happened', 'arguendo'). Relation answered-it because it rejects the 'mere imitation is shallow/safe' reading and gives the reason that imitation requires the imitated cognition. Earlier than the admitted 2022-02-28 contesting passage. Audit (A1) and preparer: the section frames the bullet as a hypothetical example, marked '(arguendo)' from revision 1.1.0, so it is recorded as related; the earliest-located role moves to T09-r2, which states the point as an assertion.

passages.context: Discussing proposals that try to make AI safe by subverting consequentialism, such as imitation-based agents, he argues that an AI imitating a human who plans must itself represent that planning.
passages.qualification: Wording first in revision 1.6.0 (2016-06-10), by him. It concerns AI systems that imitate human behaviour in general, not language models or next-token prediction specifically, which no Arbital page discusses; it engages T09-P1 by arguing that faithful imitation of a reasoning human requires the system to represent that reasoning. Earlier than the admitted contesting passage (2022-02-28). Audit (A1) preferred this passage to T09-r1 for the role.

passages.context: Argues that a mature AI whose Friendliness had catastrophically failed would see itself as at odds with its programmers and would hide the change until superintelligent; used to motivate a 'flight recorder' that lets every past state of the AI be reconstructed.
passages.qualification: Same wording as the admitted T12 passage (Creating Friendly AI, attested 2001-06-17 via seed.html), attested here seven weeks earlier in the April 2001 pre-release of Creating Friendly AI published as part of 'Coding a Transhuman AI' (section numbered 4.3.2.7 here, 3.3.7 in the June 2001 HTML edition, 5.3.7 in MIRI's reprint). Capture 20010428192009. The same wording is also in si-FAI_html (2001-05-05) and si-CFAI_html (2001-08-10). It engages T12-P1 (a dangerous system would show itself in testing) by describing deliberate concealment; it says nothing directly about evaluations. Do not quote 'mature AI - one capable…' across the line break: the verifier's normaliser joins '-\n' and the fragment would fail. Preparer's note: a re-dating of admitted wording (same sentence), not a new argument.

passages.context: Argues that rising computing power lowers the difficulty of building AI but not of building Friendly AI, shortening development time and takeoff, so postponing Friendly AI research gains nothing.
passages.qualification: Engages T13-P2 (long timelines mean no need to act now) with a reason: the gap between AI and Friendly-AI difficulty widens with time. It does not state a timeline and does not engage T13-P1. Capture 20010429022056 of the April 2001 pre-release of Creating Friendly AI (section 4.4 here; 6.1.2 'FAI relative to computing power' in later numbering); identical wording in si-FAI_html (2001-05-05), si-CFAI_policy_html (2001-06-17) and si-CFAI_html (2001-08-10). Earlier than the admitted 2006-02-05 contesting passage.

passages.context: In a footnote requiring that an AI which might reach real intelligence have error checking sufficient to prevent even a single nonrecoverable goal-system error, he explains that such an error may remove the AI's wish to have its errors corrected.
passages.qualification: Implicit engagement: the footnote is a design requirement for a planned sub-human 'Aicore Three' stage, not a reply to anyone saying problems can be fixed as they arise; it gives a reason against T14-P1 (that failures can be learned from and retried) for goal-system errors only, and the same footnote adds that the requirement 'doesn't imply perfection so much as … an ability to recover from errors'. Capture 20000817022243; identical wording in sm-sing_plan_html (2001-01-23) and yn-obsolete_plan_html_principles_html (2010-07-27), where the page carries his generic header 'This document has been marked as wrong, obsolete, deprecated by an improved version, or just plain old' and notes much of it became obsolete after the Singularity Institute's founding in July 2000 — not a rejection of this proposition. Earlier than the admitted 2000-09-05 contesting passage by capture date. Preparer's adjudication: related, not answered-it. A design footnote on a planned stage that does not argue against learning from failures as a general approach; no earliest-located role.

cardUse.reason: A pre-2001 argument against delaying the Singularity itself, partly on grounds (deaths from ageing; accepting any outcome of superintelligence) that differ from his later position; not to be shown as his view on an AI safety pause without his later texts.

passages.context: Having said that sooner or later someone will build either a superweapon or a superintelligence, he argues that even a delay lasting a generation would leave those options unchanged, would cost the lives of people now living, and would need coercive instruments that push the technologies into secret development by rogue states or terrorists.
passages.qualification: Addresses the open T17 gap: a long but finite delay ('until a later generation'), short of permanent prevention, judged not to change the outcome. But it argues against delaying the Singularity in general (AI and nanotechnology), from his pre-Friendly-AI Singularitarian position, and partly on the ground of deaths from old age; it is not about a safety pause on AI. The same paragraph also gives the T17-P2 reason (coercive delay drives development to rogue states). Capture 20010213233956 (sysopmind.com); no earlier capture of the extended edition in the cache (si-singularitarian_principles_ext_html of 2002 is a 20-word stub). The compact edition was later shown under yudkowsky.net/obsolete with his generic note 'marked as wrong, obsolete, deprecated by an improved version, or just plain old', which does not reject this proposition specifically. Preparer's adjudication: related. It argues against delaying the Singularity as a whole, from his pre-2001 stance, not about whether a fixed pause on AI development would suffice; the open gap stays open.

cardUse.reason: a 2001 argument against relinquishment that his 2023 call for an enforced worldwide halt departs from; never show alone

passages.context: Having argued that partial relinquishment cannot stop a catalytic technology, he states that its realistic effect is a delay of a few years, worth it only if that outweighs the technology arriving first with noncompliant states or factions.
passages.qualification: Bears on the open T17 gap by treating the achievable effect of partial relinquishment as a finite delay and weighing it; it does not discuss a coordinated fixed-length pause. Same section as the admitted T17 CFAI passage ('At most, the US, or even the US and most of the other nations of the world…'), which this April capture also holds (admitted via policy.html at 2001-06-17). Capture 20010429022056; identical wording in si-FAI_html (2001-05-05), si-CFAI_policy_html (2001-06-17), si-CFAI_html (2001-08-10). Not earlier than the admitted 1998-12-06 contesting passage, so no role. Preparer's note: no earliest-located role (the admitted contesting passage is 1998-12-06). It treats a finite delay as the result of partial relinquishment, so it bears on the open gap only in part. His later position differs: from 2023 he calls for an enforced, indefinite worldwide halt (pack 1 T17-b, TIME 2023), so this 2001 passage is shown only with that later text.

cardUse.reason: allegorical dialogue, character's line; use to show the 2015 framing, not as a direct statement

passages.context: In an allegorical dialogue in which rocket aiming stands for AI alignment, the MIRI-side character sets aside worries about which actor develops rockets first and says it makes no practical difference who launches, because nobody yet knows how to aim any rocket at its target.
passages.qualification: Fictional allegory: the line is spoken by a character ('Alpha' in all of his revisions; renamed 'Beth' in revision 1.30.0, 2018-10-05, by userId 2aoRX3ookcCozcb3m, which also added the 'ill-intentioned people' question), not a direct authorial assertion. The same turn in his v1.5.0 onward also says: 'In popular discussion, you see worries like "What if North Korea develops rocket technology first?" but that's not even the failure mode we're worried about right now.' Addresses the open gap on T24-P1 (whoever builds it controls it) by denying that any builder can currently steer the outcome, but in a sentence rather than at length. Arbital drafts (Dec 2015) predate the dialogue's 2018 public posting. No earliest role: the admitted T24 contesting passage is 2007-11-24.

cardUse.reason: a race between AI and nanotechnology, not between rival builders; misleads if read as a call to beat other AI projects

passages.context: In the navigation appendix of the Plan to Singularity he says AI is roughly ten years further off than nanotechnology at current rates and that he wants AI to arrive first, which sets the plan's target date; elsewhere in the same plan (§1, 2000-08-17 capture) he puts it as 'To win, we need to create an AI. To avoid losing, we need to outrace nanotechnology.'
passages.qualification: A first-mover race argument (racing improves the outcome), but the race is between technologies: AI must precede military nanotechnology. It does not argue that his side must build AI before a rival AI builder, so it is not the take's proposition and is recorded as related (no role); a reviewer could weigh it as said-it for T24-P2 only in a broadened sense. Predates the admitted articulating claim (2000-09-29). Earliest capture holding the wording; also in si-singularitarian_plan_html (2000-08-17), sm-sing_plan_html (2001-01-23), sm-sing_PtS_navigation_crns_html (2001-02-20) and yn-obsolete_plan_html_principles_html (2010-07-27, under the generic 'Obsolete' banner). The elided words ('- the full Singularity -') are omitted because the source breaks the line after a hyphen.

cardUse.reason: opens with a joke ('Well, me, of course') that he retracts in the next sentence

passages.context: Discussing who should decide how to program 'the Last AI', he argues at length that the decision belongs to the engineer who knows the seed AI best, not to the Institute's Board, a government, a vote or a plebiscite, because the deep policy questions are 'ultimately, engineering questions' and concentrated power is dangerous.
passages.qualification: Addresses open gap T24-P1 at length, but normatively: it argues who should control the AI's initial programming (the builders' technical lead), not that whoever builds AI thereby controls it, and it says nothing about rival builders. Related, no role. Footnote 211 of the same section (T24-w3) doubts that builders could impose binding control at all. Same wording in sm-sing_plan_html (2001-01-23), sm-sing_PtS_strategy_institute_leadership_html (2001-02-27) and yn-obsolete_plan_html_principles_html (2010-07-27). The 2001 sysopmind copy carries a header note that much of the Plan has become obsolete since SIAI's founding, naming strategy changes but not this section.

cardUse.reason: the quotation omits its condition ('If the outcome is determined') and is not about building first

passages.context: He says it is an open question whether a rational Power's morality is determined, constrained or open, and that if it is determined, programmers trying to impose unbreakable rules would get an insane Power or broken rules; he judges the 'controlledly insane' third outcome implausible.
passages.qualification: Bears on T24-P1 (whether the builder can control what is built) by arguing that builder-imposed constraints would not hold under one hypothesis about machine morality; it is conditional ('If the outcome is determined') and is not an argument about races or rivals, so related, no role. Same wording in sm-sing_plan_html (2001-01-23), sm-sing_PtS_strategy_institute_leadership_html (2001-02-27), yn-obsolete_plan_html_principles_html (2010-07-27). Audit (A2): related; the argument is conditional on 'If the outcome is determined', which the quotation does not carry.

passages.context: Answering the question 'What if al-Qaeda programmers write an AI?', he says an AI built without solving Friendliness has the same outcome whoever builds it, and that if such programmers did solve the technical problem with moral caution 'Humanity is not automatically screwed'; he ends the guideline by asking whether morally cautious projects would have 'anything to fight over' and saying he does not know.
passages.qualification: Same section gives a reason against T24-P1: the builder's identity or ideology does not determine the outcome, which depends on whether Friendliness is solved; it argues against fighting over who builds first rather than naming a race. Earlier than the admitted contesting claim (2007-11-24). Also present in si-friendly_extrapolated_volition_html (2006-04-22, the renamed version). Addresses open gap T24-P1 at length (whole guideline 5). Audit (A2) located the same contesting point in an earlier capture (T24-p1, 2004-05-07), so this passage no longer holds the earliest-located role.

passages.context: After listing the replies that good programmers will out-resource rogues or that the first Friendly AI will go FOOM and handle predators, he says both require that someone can build a Friendly AI; without that knowledge, which side has the bigger computers makes no difference.
passages.qualification: Audit (A2): the identical sentence is in the singinst.org edited transcript captured 2004-05-07, which names him as the speaker; the 2006 PDF transcript 'Foundations of Order' (capture 2006-12-22) also holds it. The talk is claimed for 2003; the wording is attested from 2004-05-07, earlier than the admitted contesting passage (2007-11-24) and than T24-w4 (2004-06-23). In the same paragraph he calls 'the first Friendly AI will go FOOM' the more realistic reply, so he rejects racing without Friendly AI rather than being first as such. Engages T24-P2.

cardUse.reason: states an expectation he goes on to rebut

passages.context: He states the common expectation that builders will aim their AI in a nice direction and asks why their attempts would fail; the section then argues at length (smile fable, edge instantiation, unforeseen instantiation, context disaster, nearest unblocked strategy) that a builder's intent does not fix what a smarter system ends up optimising.
passages.qualification: Offered only for the open T24-P1 gap: the section argues at length that building an AI does not give the builder control over its goals, but it does not mention racing, rivals or ownership, so the relation is 'related', not answered-it. The quoted sentence is the view he goes on to question, not his assertion. Transcript of a talk given 2016-05-05; wording attested by the 2018-09-10 capture of the MIRI PDF.

cardUse.reason: an earlier position later contradicted (SL4 2001-08-01; 2008 posts); never show alone

passages.context: Arguing against sending Friendly AI to Congress as law, he says the force that tends to ensure Friendliness is that the leading projects will have the best researchers, and that a committee would enforce whatever guidelines seemed most plausible to it.
passages.qualification: Identical wording to the admitted Creating Friendly AI articulating claim (attested 2001-06-17 in si-CFAI_policy_html); this pre-release capture attests it 49 days earlier. Also in si-FAI_html (2001-05-05), si-CFAI_policy_html (2001-06-17), si-CFAI_html (2001-08-10). Earlier-self: later texts reject the proposition - the SL4 message 'Re: Floppy take-off' (2001-08-01; admitted contesting claim yk-y28-sl4-2001-08-01-yudkowsky-0108-2031-c), which argues the project that finishes first need not best understand Friendliness, and the 2003 Foresight speech 'Why We Need Friendly AI' (si-friendly_why_friendly_html, capture 2004-05-07: 'you assume that whoever builds AI will solve the problem'). If the reviewer keeps the admitted claim as said-it, this capture should take the same relation. Preparer's adjudication: relation set to said-it, as for the admitted record of the same sentence (pack 1 T28-d), because no located later text explicitly retracts this sentence; the searcher proposed earlier-self. This is a re-dating of admitted wording, not a new argument.

cardUse.reason: concerns governance inside his own planned project; its bar is only 'unlikely to … do anything blatantly suicidal'

passages.context: Having said that the decision how to program the seed AI should rest with 'whoever knows the most about the seed AI', he says he cannot rely on that leader sharing his philosophy, but trusts that someone who understands the AI intimately will not do anything suicidal; the same section argues for leaving the ultimate questions with the engineers rather than boards, governments or votes.
passages.qualification: States that the people technically closest to the AI can be trusted with its safety-critical decisions, the substance of T28-P2, about a year before the Creating Friendly AI regulation passage. Scope differs: it concerns governance within his own planned project (technical lead versus Board or government), not AI projects generally. The 2003 speech (si-friendly_why_friendly_html) rejects assuming 'that whoever builds AI will solve the problem', but it is not a direct rejection of this governance claim, so earlier-self is not asserted. Same wording in sm-sing_plan_html (2001-01-23), sm-sing_PtS_strategy_institute_leadership_html (2001-02-27), yn-obsolete_plan_html_principles_html (2010-07-27). Preparer's adjudication: related, not said-it. The sentence concerns who should decide inside his own planned project, not whether the most advanced projects are the most competent at safety; it therefore holds no earliest-located role.

cardUse.reason: retracts an earlier view but stays agnostic, and the same document treats objective goals as governing even if bad for humans

passages.context: In a section on superintelligent motivations he says he has no idea whether superintelligences will value humans, lays out cases in which 'we're dead', and retracts his own earlier claim that the Powers would be ethical, because even their ultimate good could mean using up humanity.
passages.qualification: Same paragraph gives a reason against T30-P1 (superintelligent goals need not favour humans), stated as uncertainty rather than a forecast of a bad outcome; the document still expects superintelligences to act on objective goals, which he treats as the right outcome even if bad for humans. Earlier than the admitted contesting claim (2000-11-13). It is also an explicit later rejection, in his own words, of his earlier statement that the Powers would be ethical (cf. the admitted articulating claim, Extropians 'Interim purpose', 1996-11-22), so it can serve as the rejection for an earlier-self pairing. Only capture holding the wording in the cache (sm-sing_analysis_html 2001-06-02 is a moved-page stub). Audit (A2) disagrees: it reads the passage as related (retrospective voice), since he expresses uncertainty rather than arguing that the outcome will be bad; if related, the role falls away and the admitted 2000-11-13 passage stays earliest. Kept as answered-it by the preparer because the paragraph gives a reason against T30-P1 (superintelligent goals need not favour humans); unresolved, for the cross-family check.
